title: Who Are the Best Informal Coaches and Mentors on Your Team?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Team members often quietly mentor and coach colleagues without recognition or formal assignment, providing enormous value by sharing knowledge and helping peers navigate the organization. Yet most team leaders remain oblivious to this hidden work. Smart leaders presume some individuals excel at informal coaching and deliberately seek to identify them. Research shows that when leadership acknowledges this work and publicly recognizes those who excel at it, more informal coaching emerges throughout the team. Leaders can amplify generosity and sharing by establishing year-end awards for the best informal coach or singling out mentors during all-team meetings, signaling how important this work is. The move is straightforward: make the invisible visible, so that what goes unnoticed and unrewarded becomes a team norm everyone understands and practices.
points: Behind the scenes and without being asked, certain team members provide enormous value by informally coaching less experienced colleagues, yet this work typically goes unnoticed by leaders and unrewarded.
Smart leaders do not assume this coaching will happen naturally; they deliberately go out of their way to learn who is doing unheralded informal mentoring work on their teams.
Team members are more likely to coach and guide those below them when leadership acknowledges this work and publicly recognizes those who excel at it, creating a virtuous cycle.
Leaders who place a halo on specific team members excelling at coaching others promote more generosity and sharing throughout the entire team, increasing the number of informal coaches.

Establishing formal recognition like a year-end award for the best informal team coach or singling out mentors during all-team meetings signals how important this invisible work is and that it does not go unnoticed.
quotes: Behind the scenes, under the radar, and without being asked, team members work to improve the knowledge and skills of less experienced colleagues.
They informally coach, mentor, guide, and tutor junior members of the team, helping them navigate the organization and leading them to higher performance.

The generosity and leadership these team members display often go unnoticed and unrewarded as they do this work inconspicuously. But their colleagues, who know exactly who they are and how much value they create, hold them in the highest regard.
Not surprisingly, team members are more likely to coach and guide those below them when it is known by leadership that they are sharing their time, knowledge, and experience with others.
Leaders encourage more informal coaching of others within the team when they acknowledge the importance of this work and publicly recognize those who excel at it.

Formally recognizing them for their informal contribution is a Win-Win. Make it a point to thank them for their efforts. They make your job easier and improve the performance of the team without being asked.” Archived from Admired Leadership Field Notes (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
